LCH-5_1_6_1_3.tip: Leguminous plants mostly grown as green fodder for livestock, which also add nitrogen to the soil, e.g. clover or lucerne (alfalfa).

LCH-5_1_6_1_4.label: Root And Tuber Crops
LCH-5_1_6_1_4.tip: Crops grown for their underground roots or tubers, e.g. potatoes, sugar beet or carrots.

LCH-5_1_6_1_4_1.label: Potatoes
LCH-5_1_6_1_4_1.tip: Potato plants grown for their starchy underground tubers.

LCH-5_1_6_1_4_2.label: Sweet Potatoes
LCH-5_1_6_1_4_2.tip: A crop grown for its sweet, starchy tuberous roots; not closely related to the common potato.

LCH-5_1_6_1_4_3.label: Sugar Beet
LCH-5_1_6_1_4_3.tip: A field crop grown for its thick white root, which is processed to make table sugar.

LCH-5_1_6_1_4_4.label: Fodder Beet
LCH-5_1_6_1_4_4.tip: A large beet grown on farmland as animal feed rather than for people, e.g. to feed cattle over winter.

LCH-5_1_6_1_4_5.label: Carrot
LCH-5_1_6_1_4_5.tip: The familiar orange root vegetable, grown in fields for its edible taproot.

LCH-5_1_6_1_4_6.label: Parsnip
LCH-5_1_6_1_4_6.tip: A pale, carrot-like root vegetable grown in fields for its sweet, edible root.

LCH-5_1_6_1_4_7.label: Horseradish
LCH-5_1_6_1_4_7.tip: A plant grown for its pungent root, which is grated to make a hot condiment, e.g. horseradish sauce.

LCH-5_1_6_1_4_8.label: Radish
LCH-5_1_6_1_4_8.tip: A fast-growing vegetable cultivated for its crisp, peppery root, often eaten raw in salads.

LCH-5_1_6_1_4_9.label: Beetroot
LCH-5_1_6_1_4_9.tip: A red beet grown as a vegetable for its round, deep red edible root.

LCH-5_1_6_1_4_10.label: White Turnip
LCH-5_1_6_1_4_10.tip: A root vegetable with a white, rounded root, grown in fields for food or sometimes animal feed.

LCH-5_1_6_1_4_11.label: Celery Root
LCH-5_1_6_1_4_11.tip: Also called celeriac, a type of celery grown for its large, knobbly edible root rather than its stalks.

LCH-5_1_6_1_5.label: Bulb Vegetable Crops
LCH-5_1_6_1_5.tip: Groups vegetables grown for their edible bulbs or bulb-like stems, e.g. onions, garlic and leeks.

LCH-5_1_6_1_5_1.label: Onions
LCH-5_1_6_1_5_1.tip: A common bulb vegetable grown in fields for its layered, strongly flavoured bulb used in cooking.

LCH-5_1_6_1_5_2.label: Garlic
LCH-5_1_6_1_5_2.tip: A bulb crop grown for its pungent cloves, widely used to flavour food.

LCH-5_1_6_1_5_3.label: Leeks
LCH-5_1_6_1_5_3.tip: A mild, onion-related vegetable grown for its long white and green stem, e.g. used in soups.

LCH-5_1_6_1_6.label: Cole Crops, Brassica oleracea
LCH-5_1_6_1_6.tip: Groups vegetables bred from the wild cabbage plant, e.g. cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts.

LCH-5_1_6_1_6_1.label: White, Green, Red Cabbage
LCH-5_1_6_1_6_1.tip: Head-forming cabbages with white, green or red leaves, grown in fields for fresh use or sauerkraut.

LCH-5_1_6_1_6_2.label: Brussels Sprout
LCH-5_1_6_1_6_2.tip: A cabbage relative grown for the small leafy buds that form along its tall stem.

LCH-5_1_6_1_6_3.label: Stem Cabbage, Kohlrabi
LCH-5_1_6_1_6_3.tip: A cabbage relative grown for its swollen, round stem eaten as a vegetable, known as kohlrabi.

LCH-5_1_6_1_6_4.label: Cauliflower
LCH-5_1_6_1_6_4.tip: A cabbage relative grown for its dense white head of undeveloped flower buds.

LCH-5_1_6_1_6_5.label: Broccoli
LCH-5_1_6_1_6_5.tip: A cabbage relative grown for its green heads of flower buds and stalks.

LCH-5_1_6_1_6_6.label: Savoy Cabbage
LCH-5_1_6_1_6_6.tip: A type of cabbage with crinkled, wrinkly green leaves, grown as a winter vegetable.

LCH-5_1_6_1_7.label: Leaf, Stalk, Flowering Vegetable Crops
LCH-5_1_6_1_7.tip: Groups vegetables grown for their leaves, stalks or flower parts, e.g. lettuce, spinach, asparagus and artichoke.

LCH-5_1_6_1_7_1.label: Lettuces, Salads
LCH-5_1_6_1_7_1.tip: Leafy vegetables grown to be eaten fresh, e.g. lettuce and other salad greens.

LCH-5_1_6_1_7_2.label: Asparagus
LCH-5_1_6_1_7_2.tip: A perennial vegetable grown for its young shoots (spears), harvested in spring.

LCH-5_1_6_1_7_3.label: Spinach
LCH-5_1_6_1_7_3.tip: A leafy green vegetable grown for its tender, dark green leaves.

LCH-5_1_6_1_7_4.label: Rods Celery
LCH-5_1_6_1_7_4.tip: Celery grown for its long, crunchy leaf stalks, as opposed to celery grown for its root.

LCH-5_1_6_1_7_5.label: Rhubarb
LCH-5_1_6_1_7_5.tip: A perennial plant grown for its thick, sour red or green stalks, often used in desserts.

LCH-5_1_6_1_7_6.label: Artichoke
LCH-5_1_6_1_7_6.tip: A thistle-like plant grown for its large, edible flower buds.

LCH-5_1_6_1_7_7.label: Romanesco
LCH-5_1_6_1_7_7.tip: A cauliflower-like vegetable with lime-green, spiral-shaped florets, grown for its edible head.

LCH-5_1_6_1_8.label: Fruiting Vegetable Crops
LCH-5_1_6_1_8.tip: Groups vegetable plants grown for their fruits, e.g. tomatoes, peppers and eggplants.

LCH-5_1_6_1_8_1.label: Tomato
LCH-5_1_6_1_8_1.tip: A widely grown vegetable plant cultivated for its juicy red fruits, in open fields or greenhouses.

LCH-5_1_6_1_8_2.label: Bell Pepper
LCH-5_1_6_1_8_2.tip: Sweet, mild peppers grown for their large, colourful fruits, e.g. red, yellow or green peppers.

LCH-5_1_6_1_8_3.label: Chili Pepper
LCH-5_1_6_1_8_3.tip: Peppers grown for their small, hot-tasting fruits, used fresh, dried or as spice.

LCH-5_1_6_1_8_4.label: Eggplant
LCH-5_1_6_1_8_4.tip: Also called aubergine, a plant grown for its glossy, usually purple fruit eaten as a vegetable.

LCH-5_1_6_1_9.label: Cucurbit Crops
LCH-5_1_6_1_9.tip: Groups crops of the gourd family that grow on trailing vines, e.g. cucumbers, zucchini, melons and pumpkins.

LCH-5_1_6_1_9_1.label: Cucumbers
LCH-5_1_6_1_9_1.tip: A vine crop grown for its long green fruits, eaten fresh or pickled.

LCH-5_1_6_1_9_2.label: Zucchini
LCH-5_1_6_1_9_2.tip: Also called courgette, a summer squash grown for its young green fruits.

LCH-5_1_6_1_9_3.label: Melons
LCH-5_1_6_1_9_3.tip: Vine crops grown for their large, sweet fruits, e.g. watermelon or cantaloupe.

LCH-5_1_6_1_9_4.label: Pumpkins
LCH-5_1_6_1_9_4.tip: Vine crops grown for their large, usually orange fruits, used for food, animal feed or decoration.

LCH-5_1_6_1_10.label: Oilseed or Fibre Crops
LCH-5_1_6_1_10.tip: Groups field crops grown mainly for oil from their seeds or for plant fibres, e.g. sunflower, rapeseed, cotton and hemp. Some industrial crops such as tobacco and hops also sit here.

LCH-5_1_6_1_10_1.label: Tobacco
LCH-5_1_6_1_10_1.tip: A field crop grown for its large leaves, which are dried and used to make cigarettes and other tobacco products.

LCH-5_1_6_1_10_2.label: Hops
LCH-5_1_6_1_10_2.tip: A climbing plant grown on tall wire frames for its cone-shaped flowers, used mainly to flavour beer.

LCH-5_1_6_1_10_3.label: Rape and Turnip Rape
LCH-5_1_6_1_10_3.tip: Oilseed crops of the cabbage family, recognised by bright yellow fields in spring, grown for oil, e.g. rapeseed (canola).

LCH-5_1_6_1_10_4.label: Sunflower
LCH-5_1_6_1_10_4.tip: A tall plant with large yellow flower heads, grown for its seeds, which are pressed for oil or eaten.

LCH-5_1_6_1_10_5.label: Linseed, Oil Flax
LCH-5_1_6_1_10_5.tip: Flax varieties grown mainly for their seeds, which yield linseed oil and are used as food.

LCH-5_1_6_1_10_6.label: Cotton
LCH-5_1_6_1_10_6.tip: A shrubby crop grown for the soft white fibres around its seeds, used to make textiles.

LCH-5_1_6_1_10_7.label: Flax
LCH-5_1_6_1_10_7.tip: A slender plant grown for the fibres in its stems, used to make linen.

LCH-5_1_6_1_10_8.label: Hemp
LCH-5_1_6_1_10_8.tip: A fast-growing plant cultivated for strong stem fibres and seeds, e.g. for rope, textiles or oil.

LCH-5_1_6_1_10_9.label: Other Oilseed or Fibre Crops
LCH-5_1_6_1_10_9.tip: Oil or fibre crops that do not fit the more specific types listed alongside, such as sunflower or cotton.

LCH-5_1_6_1_11.label: Aromatic, Medicinal, Culinary Herbs
LCH-5_1_6_1_11.tip: Herbs grown in fields for scent, medicine or cooking, e.g. lavender, chamomile, parsley or basil.

LCH-5_1_6_1_12.label: Flowers and Ornamental Plants
LCH-5_1_6_1_12.tip: Plants grown commercially for their flowers or decorative value, e.g. tulips, roses or bedding plants.

LCH-5_1_6_1_13.label: Strawberries
LCH-5_1_6_1_13.tip: Low-growing plants cultivated in fields or tunnels for their sweet red fruit, treated here as an arable crop.

LCH-5_1_6_1_14.label: Sugarcane
LCH-5_1_6_1_14.tip: A tall tropical grass grown for its thick stems, which are crushed to extract juice for sugar or biofuel.

LCH-5_1_6_1_99.label: Other Arable Crops
LCH-5_1_6_1_99.tip: Arable crops, grown on regularly ploughed or tilled land, that do not fit any of the more specific crop groups listed.

LCH-5_1_6_2.label: Meadow Grasses And Herbs
LCH-5_1_6_2.tip: Grasses and herbaceous plants grown or managed on meadows, mainly for hay, silage or grazing.

LCH-5_1_6_3.label: Permanent Crops
LCH-5_1_6_3.tip: Groups crops that stay in the ground for many years and are harvested repeatedly, e.g. orchards, vineyards and olive groves.

LCH-5_1_6_3_1.label: Pome Fruits
LCH-5_1_6_3_1.tip: Groups orchard fruits with a fleshy body around a core of small seeds, e.g. apples and pears.

LCH-5_1_6_3_1_1.label: Apple
LCH-5_1_6_3_1_1.tip: Orchard trees grown for apples, one of the most common fruit crops in Europe.

LCH-5_1_6_3_1_2.label: Pear
LCH-5_1_6_3_1_2.tip: Orchard trees grown for pears, sweet fruits with a seed core similar to apples.

LCH-5_1_6_3_1_3.label: Quince
LCH-5_1_6_3_1_3.tip: Small trees grown for quince, a hard, fragrant fruit usually cooked into jams or jellies.

LCH-5_1_6_3_1_4.label: Medlar
LCH-5_1_6_3_1_4.tip: Small trees grown for medlar, a brownish fruit traditionally eaten once it softens after harvest.

LCH-5_1_6_3_1_5.label: Pomegranate
LCH-5_1_6_3_1_5.tip: Shrubs or small trees grown for pomegranates, round fruits filled with juicy red seeds.

LCH-5_1_6_3_2.label: Drupes, Stone-Like Fruits
LCH-5_1_6_3_2.tip: Groups tree fruits with soft flesh around a single hard stone, e.g. cherries, plums, peaches and apricots.

LCH-5_1_6_3_2_1.label: Sweet Cherry
LCH-5_1_6_3_2_1.tip: Orchard trees grown for sweet cherries, eaten fresh as dessert fruit.

LCH-5_1_6_3_2_2.label: Sour Cherry
LCH-5_1_6_3_2_2.tip: Trees grown for sour cherries, tart fruits mostly used for juice, jam or baking.

LCH-5_1_6_3_2_3.label: Plum
LCH-5_1_6_3_2_3.tip: Orchard trees grown for plums, juicy stone fruits eaten fresh, dried as prunes or distilled.

LCH-5_1_6_3_2_4.label: Mirabelle, Spilling
LCH-5_1_6_3_2_4.tip: Trees grown for small plum-type fruits, e.g. the yellow mirabelle plum.

LCH-5_1_6_3_2_5.label: Peach, Nectarine
LCH-5_1_6_3_2_5.tip: Orchard trees grown for peaches and nectarines, juicy stone fruits; nectarines have smooth skin.

LCH-5_1_6_3_2_6.label: Apricot
LCH-5_1_6_3_2_6.tip: Orchard trees grown for apricots, small orange stone fruits eaten fresh or dried.

LCH-5_1_6_3_2_7.label: Avocado
LCH-5_1_6_3_2_7.tip: Trees grown for avocados, creamy green fruits with one large seed.

LCH-5_1_6_3_2_8.label: Mango
LCH-5_1_6_3_2_8.tip: Tropical trees grown for mangoes, sweet fruits with orange flesh around a large flat stone.

LCH-5_1_6_3_2_9.label: Litchi
LCH-5_1_6_3_2_9.tip: Subtropical trees grown for lychees, small fruits with rough red skin and white, juicy flesh.

LCH-5_1_6_3_2_10.label: Date Fruit
LCH-5_1_6_3_2_10.tip: Date palms grown in plantations for their sweet fruits, e.g. in desert oases.

LCH-5_1_6_3_2_11.label: Oil Palm
LCH-5_1_6_3_2_11.tip: Tropical palms grown in plantations for their fruit, which is pressed to produce palm oil.

LCH-5_1_6_3_3.label: Nuts
LCH-5_1_6_3_3.tip: Groups trees and shrubs grown for their edible nuts, e.g. walnuts, hazelnuts and almonds.

LCH-5_1_6_3_3_1.label: Walnuts
LCH-5_1_6_3_3_1.tip: Trees grown for walnuts, hard-shelled nuts used as food and for oil.

LCH-5_1_6_3_3_2.label: Chestnuts
LCH-5_1_6_3_3_2.tip: Sweet chestnut trees grown for their edible nuts, often roasted in autumn.

LCH-5_1_6_3_3_3.label: Hazelnuts
LCH-5_1_6_3_3_3.tip: Shrubs or small trees grown for hazelnuts, e.g. used in chocolate spreads and baking.

LCH-5_1_6_3_3_4.label: Cashew Nuts
LCH-5_1_6_3_3_4.tip: Tropical trees grown for cashew nuts, which hang below a fleshy fruit called the cashew apple.

LCH-5_1_6_3_3_5.label: Brazil Nuts
LCH-5_1_6_3_3_5.tip: Tall tropical trees grown or harvested for Brazil nuts, large seeds packed inside a hard pod.

LCH-5_1_6_3_3_6.label: Pekka Nuts
LCH-5_1_6_3_3_6.tip: Likely refers to pecan nuts, grown on large trees for their rich, edible nuts.

LCH-5_1_6_3_3_7.label: Pistachios
LCH-5_1_6_3_3_7.tip: Trees grown in warm, dry areas for pistachios, green nuts in a split shell.

LCH-5_1_6_3_3_8.label: Almond
LCH-5_1_6_3_3_8.tip: Orchard trees grown for almonds, nuts eaten whole or used in baking and almond milk.

LCH-5_1_6_3_3_9.label: Coconuts
LCH-5_1_6_3_3_9.tip: Coconut palms grown in tropical plantations for their large nuts, used for food, oil and fibre.

LCH-5_1_6_3_4.label: Citrus Fruits
LCH-5_1_6_3_4.tip: Groups trees grown for juicy, segmented fruits with aromatic peel, e.g. oranges, lemons and mandarins.

LCH-5_1_6_3_4_1.label: Oranges
LCH-5_1_6_3_4_1.tip: Citrus trees grown for oranges, the most widely grown citrus fruit, eaten fresh or juiced.

LCH-5_1_6_3_4_2.label: Lemons
LCH-5_1_6_3_4_2.tip: Citrus trees grown for lemons, sour yellow fruits used for juice and flavouring.

LCH-5_1_6_3_4_3.label: Limes
LCH-5_1_6_3_4_3.tip: Citrus trees grown for limes, small green sour fruits used in cooking and drinks.

LCH-5_1_6_3_4_4.label: Pomelos
LCH-5_1_6_3_4_4.tip: Citrus trees grown for pomelos, the largest citrus fruit, with thick peel and mild flesh.

LCH-5_1_6_3_4_5.label: Grapefruits
LCH-5_1_6_3_4_5.tip: Citrus trees grown for grapefruits, large fruits with a slightly bitter taste.

LCH-5_1_6_3_4_6.label: Mandarine
LCH-5_1_6_3_4_6.tip: Citrus trees grown for mandarins, small, easy-to-peel sweet oranges.

LCH-5_1_6_3_4_7.label: Clementine
LCH-5_1_6_3_4_7.tip: Citrus trees grown for clementines, small, usually seedless mandarin-type fruits.

LCH-5_1_6_3_5.label: Berry Crops
LCH-5_1_6_3_5.tip: Groups shrubs and plants grown for small, soft fruits, e.g. raspberries, currants and blueberries.

LCH-5_1_6_3_5_1.label: Raspberries
LCH-5_1_6_3_5_1.tip: Cane plants grown for raspberries, soft red berries eaten fresh or frozen.

LCH-5_1_6_3_5_2.label: Blackberries
LCH-5_1_6_3_5_2.tip: Thorny or thornless canes grown for blackberries, dark juicy berries.

LCH-5_1_6_3_5_3.label: Currants
LCH-5_1_6_3_5_3.tip: Shrubs grown for currants, small red, white or black berries used in juice and jam.

LCH-5_1_6_3_5_4.label: Gooseberries
LCH-5_1_6_3_5_4.tip: Spiny shrubs grown for gooseberries, tart green or reddish berries.

LCH-5_1_6_3_5_5.label: Blueberries
LCH-5_1_6_3_5_5.tip: Shrubs grown for blueberries, small sweet blue berries, often on acidic soils.

LCH-5_1_6_3_5_6.label: Cranberries
LCH-5_1_6_3_5_6.tip: Low creeping plants grown for cranberries, sour red berries, often in flooded beds or bogs.

LCH-5_1_6_3_5_7.label: Juniper
LCH-5_1_6_3_5_7.tip: Evergreen shrubs grown for juniper berries, used as a spice and to flavour gin.

LCH-5_1_6_3_5_8.label: Elderberries
LCH-5_1_6_3_5_8.tip: Shrubs grown for elderberries and elderflowers, used for syrups, juice and wine.

LCH-5_1_6_3_5_9.label: Cornel
LCH-5_1_6_3_5_9.tip: Shrubs or small trees grown for cornels (cornelian cherries), small red, tart fruits.

LCH-5_1_6_3_5_10.label: Passion Fruit
LCH-5_1_6_3_5_10.tip: Climbing vines grown in warm regions for passion fruit, with pulpy, aromatic seeds.

LCH-5_1_6_3_6.label: Grapes
LCH-5_1_6_3_6.tip: Vineyards growing grapevines for wine, table grapes or raisins.

LCH-5_1_6_3_7.label: Olives
LCH-5_1_6_3_7.tip: Olive groves with long-lived trees grown for olives, eaten or pressed into olive oil.

LCH-5_1_6_3_8.label: Other Fleshy Fruits
LCH-5_1_6_3_8.tip: Groups other trees and plants grown for soft, juicy fruits, e.g. bananas, figs, kiwis and papayas.

LCH-5_1_6_3_8_1.label: Banana
LCH-5_1_6_3_8_1.tip: Large tropical plants grown in plantations for bunches of bananas.

LCH-5_1_6_3_8_2.label: Fig Fruit
LCH-5_1_6_3_8_2.tip: Trees grown for figs, soft sweet fruits eaten fresh or dried.

LCH-5_1_6_3_8_3.label: Kiwi
LCH-5_1_6_3_8_3.tip: Climbing vines grown on trellises for kiwi fruit, with brown fuzzy skin and green flesh.

LCH-5_1_6_3_8_4.label: Papaya
LCH-5_1_6_3_8_4.tip: Tropical plants grown for papayas, large fruits with orange flesh and black seeds.

LCH-5_1_6_3_8_5.label: Ananas
LCH-5_1_6_3_8_5.tip: Pineapple, a tropical plant grown in fields for its large, spiky, sweet fruit.

LCH-5_1_6_3_8_6.label: Custard Apple
LCH-5_1_6_3_8_6.tip: Tropical trees grown for custard apples, fruits with sweet, creamy white flesh.

LCH-5_1_6_3_8_7.label: Prickly Pear
LCH-5_1_6_3_8_7.tip: Cactus plants grown for their edible fruits, known as prickly pears, common in Mediterranean areas.

LCH-5_1_6_3_8_8.label: Persimmon
LCH-5_1_6_3_8_8.tip: Trees grown for persimmons (kaki), orange fruits that are sweet when fully ripe.

LCH-5_1_6_3_9.label: Exotic Aromatic and Spice Crops
LCH-5_1_6_3_9.tip: Groups tropical perennial plants grown for drinks, spices and flavourings, e.g. coffee, cocoa, vanilla and pepper.

LCH-5_1_6_3_9_1.label: Coffee Bush
LCH-5_1_6_3_9_1.tip: Shrubs grown in tropical plantations for coffee beans, the seeds inside their red berries.

LCH-5_1_6_3_9_2.label: Cocoa Tree
LCH-5_1_6_3_9_2.tip: Tropical trees grown for cocoa beans, the raw material for chocolate.

LCH-5_1_6_3_9_3.label: Pepper
LCH-5_1_6_3_9_3.tip: Climbing vines grown for peppercorns, which are dried to make black, white or green pepper.

LCH-5_1_6_3_9_4.label: Cinnamon Tree
LCH-5_1_6_3_9_4.tip: Tropical trees grown for their inner bark, which is dried to make the spice cinnamon.

LCH-5_1_6_3_9_5.label: Vanilla
LCH-5_1_6_3_9_5.tip: A climbing orchid grown in the tropics for its seed pods, cured to make vanilla.

LCH-5_1_6_3_9_6.label: Cloves
LCH-5_1_6_3_9_6.tip: Tropical trees grown for their dried flower buds, used as the spice cloves.

LCH-5_1_6_3_9_7.label: Cardamom
LCH-5_1_6_3_9_7.tip: A tropical plant of the ginger family grown for its aromatic seed pods, used as a spice.

LCH-5_1_6_3_9_8.label: Ginger
LCH-5_1_6_3_9_8.tip: A tropical plant grown for its spicy underground stem (rhizome), used fresh or dried in cooking.

LCH-5_1_6_3_10.label: Leaf Crops from Woody Plants
LCH-5_1_6_3_10.tip: Groups shrubs and trees grown so that their leaves can be harvested, e.g. tea bushes.

LCH-5_1_6_3_10_1.label: Tea Bush
LCH-5_1_6_3_10_1.tip: Evergreen shrubs grown on plantations, often on hillsides, for leaves used to make tea.

LCH-5_1_6_3_10_2.label: Coca Bush
LCH-5_1_6_3_10_2.tip: Shrubs grown mainly in the Andes for coca leaves, which are chewed, brewed or processed.

LCH-5_1_6_3_10_3.label: Mate Tree
LCH-5_1_6_3_10_3.tip: South American trees grown for leaves used to brew mate, a caffeinated herbal drink.

LCH-5_1_6_3_11.label: Woody Plant Nursery
LCH-5_1_6_3_11.tip: Land where young trees and shrubs are raised for sale or replanting, e.g. a tree nursery for gardens or forestry.

LCH-5_1_6_3_12.label: Christmas Trees
LCH-5_1_6_3_12.tip: Plantations of young conifers, e.g. fir or spruce, grown to be cut and sold as Christmas trees.

LCH-5_1_6_3_13.label: Herbaceous Biomass Crops
LCH-5_1_6_3_13.tip: Long-lived, non-woody plants grown to produce biomass for energy or materials, e.g. Miscanthus, Silphium or Sorghum.

LCH-5_1_6_3_14.label: Woody Biomass Crops
LCH-5_1_6_3_14.tip: Fast-growing trees or shrubs planted to produce wood biomass, e.g. willow or poplar harvested in short cycles.

LCH-5_1_6_3_99.label: Other Permanent Crops
LCH-5_1_6_3_99.tip: Permanent crops, which stay in the ground for many years, that do not fit any of the more specific groups listed.

LCH-5_1_6_4.label: Mushrooms
LCH-5_1_6_4.tip: Cultivated mushrooms, usually grown indoors on special substrates, e.g. button mushrooms or oyster mushrooms.

LCH-5_1_6_5.label: Aquatic Crops
LCH-5_1_6_5.tip: Groups crops grown in water rather than on dry land, e.g. cultivated algae.

LCH-5_1_6_5_1.label: Algae Crops
LCH-5_1_6_5_1.tip: Algae farmed in ponds, tanks or the sea, e.g. seaweed or microalgae used for food, feed or fuel.

LCH-5_1_6_98.label: Fallow Land
LCH-5_1_6_98.tip: Former farmland left uncultivated for at least 3 years or for good, with no crop cover and no longer part of a crop rotation.

LCH-5_1_6_99.label: Unspecified Crop
LCH-5_1_6_99.tip: Use when a parcel is clearly being farmed, but the crop species growing on it is not known.

LCH-5_1_7.label: Plant Growth Stage
LCH-5_1_7.tip: Groups the stages a crop passes through during the season, from sowing and germination through flowering and ripening to after harvest.

LCH-5_1_7_1.label: Sowing The Seeds
LCH-5_1_7_1.tip: The stage just after seeds are put in the field, before any sprouts or plant growth can be seen.

LCH-5_1_7_2.label: Germination, Sprouting
LCH-5_1_7_2.tip: The early stage when seeds start to grow and the first sprouts appear.

LCH-5_1_7_3.label: Vegetative Phase
LCH-5_1_7_3.tip: The stage when sprouts grow into young plants, putting out leaves and shoots, e.g. cereals forming side shoots (tillering).

LCH-5_1_7_4.label: Reproductive Phase
LCH-5_1_7_4.tip: The stage when crops form heads, ears or flowers, e.g. wheat producing ears.

LCH-5_1_7_5.label: Ripening Phase
LCH-5_1_7_5.tip: The stage when crops form fruit or grain and mature, after which the plants begin to age and die back.

LCH-5_1_7_6.label: Harvested Empty Field
LCH-5_1_7_6.tip: A field that has been harvested and left bare, with no crop leftovers and no regrowth of weeds yet.

LCH-5_1_7_7.label: Crop Residues
LCH-5_1_7_7.tip: A harvested field where leftovers remain, e.g. straw, stubble or dropped fruit. It can occur together with resprouting on the field.

LCH-5_1_7_8.label: Resprouting on Harvested Field
LCH-5_1_7_8.tip: A harvested field turning green again as weeds or spilled crop seeds sprout on their own. It can occur together with crop residues.

LCH-5_1_8.label: Crop Season
LCH-5_1_8.tip: Groups descriptions of when in the year crops are grown, e.g. summer or winter season, and how many seasons a field has.

LCH-5_1_8_1.label: Crop Season Ongoing
LCH-5_1_8_1.tip: Indicates that a crop is currently growing on the land and its growing season has not yet ended.

LCH-5_1_8_2.label: Summer Crop Season
LCH-5_1_8_2.tip: Crops sown in spring and grown through the warm months, e.g. maize harvested in late summer or autumn.

LCH-5_1_8_3.label: Winter Crop Season
LCH-5_1_8_3.tip: Crops sown in autumn that stay in the field over winter, e.g. winter wheat harvested the following summer.

LCH-5_1_8_4.label: Year-round Crop Season
LCH-5_1_8_4.tip: Crops grown continuously throughout the whole year rather than in a single season.

LCH-5_1_8_5.label: Number Of Crop Seasons
LCH-5_1_8_5.tip: The number of separate crop growing seasons that take place on the same land, typically counted per year.

LCH-5_1_9.label: Crop Rotation Element
LCH-5_1_9.tip: Groups the roles a crop can play in a crop rotation, such as main crop, follow-on crop, companion crop or cover crop.

LCH-5_1_9_1.label: Main Crop
LCH-5_1_9_1.tip: The first and main crop of the year, usually sown after the previous year's harvest, normally giving the highest yield.

LCH-5_1_9_2.label: Secondary Crop
LCH-5_1_9_2.tip: A second or third crop sown after the year's main crop is harvested; its yield is usually lower than if sown the previous autumn.

LCH-5_1_9_3.label: Side Crop
LCH-5_1_9_3.tip: An extra crop grown at the same time alongside the main or secondary crop, e.g. to improve soil or biodiversity, and also harvested.

LCH-5_1_9_4.label: Cover Crop
LCH-5_1_9_4.tip: A follow-on crop grown mainly to protect and enrich the soil, e.g. against erosion, rather than for harvest value.

LCH-5_1_10.label: Cultivation Strategy
LCH-5_1_10.tip: Groups overall approaches to farming and the bundle of methods they involve, e.g. conventional or organic farming.

LCH-5_1_10_1.label: Conventional Farming
LCH-5_1_10_1.tip: Farming that relies on industrial fertilizers, herbicides, pesticides and heavy machinery to get the highest possible yields.

LCH-5_1_10_2.label: Organic Farming
LCH-5_1_10_2.tip: Farming that avoids industrial fertilizers and pesticides, using natural fertilizers such as green manure and biological or mechanical pest control.

LCH-5_1_11.label: Grazing
LCH-5_1_11.tip: Groups information on whether land is grazed by livestock and how intensively, following the EU farm subsidy system (IACS).

LCH-5_1_11_1.label: Grazing Intensity
LCH-5_1_11_1.tip: Groups levels describing how heavily land is grazed by animals, from no grazing to grazing of unknown or low intensity.

LCH-5_1_11_1_1.label: No Grazing
LCH-5_1_11_1_1.tip: Land where no grazing by livestock has been observed.

LCH-5_1_11_1_2.label: Grazing Present, Intensity Unspecified
LCH-5_1_11_1_2.tip: Land where livestock graze, but how many animals or how intensively is not known.

LCH-5_1_11_1_3.label: Extensive, Freerange Grazing
LCH-5_1_11_1_3.tip: Low-intensity grazing with two or fewer livestock units per hectare, e.g. a few cattle roaming freely on pasture.

LCH-5_1_11_1_4.label: Intensive Grazing
LCH-5_1_11_1_4.tip: Pasture carrying a heavy load of animals, defined here as more than 2 livestock units per hectare, e.g. a field densely stocked with dairy cows.

LCH-5_1_11_2.label: Grazing Lifestock per ha
LCH-5_1_11_2.tip: Measures how many grazing animals, counted in livestock units, are kept on each hectare of a particular plot of land.

LCH-5_1_11_3.label: Grazing Cycle
LCH-5_1_11_3.tip: Groups the ways grazing is spread over the year, from year-round use of pasture to seasonal, rotational or only occasional grazing.

LCH-5_1_11_3_1.label: All Year-round Grazing
LCH-5_1_11_3_1.tip: Animals graze the land throughout the whole year rather than only in certain seasons, e.g. hardy sheep kept outdoors in all months.

LCH-5_1_11_3_2.label: Seasonal Grazing
LCH-5_1_11_3_2.tip: Animals graze the land only during part of the year, e.g. cattle taken to summer pastures in the mountains.

LCH-5_1_11_3_3.label: Rotational Grazing, Paddocks
LCH-5_1_11_3_3.tip: Livestock are moved in turns between fenced sections of pasture (paddocks), so each section gets time to regrow before being grazed again.

LCH-5_1_11_3_4.label: Occasional Grazing
LCH-5_1_11_3_4.tip: Land that animals graze only now and then, without a regular schedule, e.g. a meadow used for livestock in some years.

LCH-5_1_11_3_5.label: Unmanaged Natural Grazing
LCH-5_1_11_3_5.tip: Grazing that happens without human management, e.g. wild or free-roaming animals feeding on natural vegetation.

LCH-5_1_11_4.label: Grazing Routine
LCH-5_1_11_4.tip: Groups the times of day when animals are out grazing: during daytime, at night, or around the clock.

LCH-5_1_11_4_1.label: Day Grazing
LCH-5_1_11_4_1.tip: Animals are put out to graze during the day and kept in a barn or enclosure overnight.

LCH-5_1_11_4_2.label: Night Grazing
LCH-5_1_11_4_2.tip: Animals graze only during the night, and are kept elsewhere during the daytime.

LCH-5_1_11_4_3.label: Day and Night Grazing
LCH-5_1_11_4_3.tip: Animals stay out on the pasture and graze both by day and by night.

LCH-5_1_11_5.label: Lifestock Species Type
LCH-5_1_11_5.tip: Groups the kinds of animals that graze on a piece of land, such as cattle, sheep, goats, horses or poultry.

LCH-5_1_11_5_1.label: Cattle
LCH-5_1_11_5_1.tip: Land grazed by cows, bulls or other cattle, e.g. a pasture used by beef or dairy herds.

LCH-5_1_11_5_2.label: Horses
LCH-5_1_11_5_2.tip: Land grazed by horses, e.g. a paddock or meadow where horses are kept.

LCH-5_1_11_5_3.label: Deer
LCH-5_1_11_5_3.tip: Land grazed by deer, e.g. a fenced area where deer are farmed or kept.

LCH-5_1_11_5_4.label: Pigs, Boars
LCH-5_1_11_5_4.tip: Land where pigs or wild boars graze and root, e.g. outdoor pig farming in woodland or fields.

LCH-5_1_11_5_5.label: Sheep
LCH-5_1_11_5_5.tip: Land grazed by sheep, e.g. upland pastures or hillsides used for sheep farming.

LCH-5_1_11_5_6.label: Goats
LCH-5_1_11_5_6.tip: Land grazed by goats, e.g. rough scrubby slopes used for goat herding.

LCH-5_1_11_5_7.label: Poultry
LCH-5_1_11_5_7.tip: Land where chickens, ducks, geese or other farm birds feed outdoors, e.g. a free-range poultry run.

LCH-5_1_11_5_8.label: Other Grazing Animals
LCH-5_1_11_5_8.tip: Grazing animals not listed separately, e.g. donkeys, llamas or alpacas.

LCH-5_2.label: Forest Land Management
LCH-5_2.tip: Groups the ways woodland is managed: tree ages, species mix, harvesting and replanting methods, and what the wood is used for.

LCH-5_2_1.label: Forest Age Structure
LCH-5_2_1.tip: Describes how tree ages are mixed within a forest plot, which reflects how it has been planted, managed and harvested.

LCH-5_2_1_1.label: Even-Aged Stands
LCH-5_2_1_1.tip: A forest plot where all trees are about the same age, usually because they were planted together, e.g. a uniform spruce plantation.

LCH-5_2_1_2.label: Uneven-Aged Stands
LCH-5_2_1_2.tip: A forest plot containing trees of different ages growing side by side.

LCH-5_2_1_3.label: All-Aged Stands, Old-Growth Forest
LCH-5_2_1_3.tip: Forest made mostly of self-sown native trees whose ages and species mix come from natural growth, e.g. old woodland in a strict forest reserve.

LCH-5_2_2.label: Forest Age Stage
LCH-5_2_2.tip: Groups forests by roughly how old the trees are at the time of observation, from seedlings to mature trees.

LCH-5_2_2_1.label: Seedlings
LCH-5_2_2_1.tip: Very young trees in their first years of growth, roughly up to about 5 years old, e.g. a freshly replanted clearing.

LCH-5_2_2_2.label: Young or Mid-Aged Trees
LCH-5_2_2_2.tip: Trees in an early growth stage, roughly 5 to 15 years old as a rough guide, no longer seedlings but not yet fully grown.

LCH-5_2_2_3.label: Grown-Up or Mature Trees
LCH-5_2_2_3.tip: Fully grown trees, roughly 20 years and older as a guide; a tree counts as mature once it starts producing flowers or fruit.

LCH-5_2_3.label: Forest Composition
LCH-5_2_3.tip: Indicates whether a forest plot contains a mixture of tree species or consists mainly of one species.

LCH-5_2_3_1.label: Mixed Forest Stands
LCH-5_2_3_1.tip: Forest where several tree species grow together, e.g. oak, beech and hornbeam in the same stand.

LCH-5_2_3_2.label: Unmixed Forest Stands
LCH-5_2_3_2.tip: Forest made up mostly of a single tree species, whether planted as a monoculture or growing that way naturally, e.g. a pure pine stand.

LCH-5_2_4.label: Forestry Practice
LCH-5_2_4.tip: Groups the main overall strategies for growing and harvesting woodland, such as coppice, high forest, or a mix of the two.

LCH-5_2_4_1.label: Coppice, Low Forest
LCH-5_2_4_1.tip: Traditionally managed, usually broadleaved woodland whose trees are cut back every 15 to 25 years and regrow new shoots from the stumps.

LCH-5_2_4_2.label: Coppice-Standard Combination
LCH-5_2_4_2.tip: Woodland combining coppice, regularly cut back to the stumps, with taller trees left to grow into high forest above it.

LCH-5_2_4_3.label: High Forest
LCH-5_2_4_3.tip: Woodland of tall, straight-stemmed trees grown from seed or planted seedlings, usually forming a closed canopy when mature, e.g. a beech or spruce forest.

LCH-5_2_5.label: Forestry Rotation System
LCH-5_2_5.tip: Groups forests by how long trees are grown before they are felled, from very short cycles to continuous forest cover.

LCH-5_2_5_1.label: Short Rotation Coppice (SRC) Plantation
LCH-5_2_5_1.tip: Very dense plantings of fast-growing trees, usually willow or poplar, cut every 2 to 5 years and left to resprout from the stumps.

LCH-5_2_5_2.label: Short Rotation Forestry (SRF) Plantation
LCH-5_2_5_2.tip: Trees planted and felled once they reach about 10 to 20 cm trunk diameter, typically after 6 to 20 years, often for energy wood.

LCH-5_2_5_3.label: Intermediate or Long Rotation Forestry
LCH-5_2_5_3.tip: The most common forest management cycle, where trees are harvested once stands are around 40 to 50 years old or older.

LCH-5_2_5_4.label: Continuous Cover Forestry
LCH-5_2_5_4.tip: Forest kept permanently wooded by harvesting individual trees rather than clear cutting, usually leaving a mix of species and ages.

LCH-5_2_6.label: Forest Rejuvenation
LCH-5_2_6.tip: Groups the ways a forest renews itself after harvest or disturbance, either through planting and sowing by people or through natural regrowth.

LCH-5_2_6_1.label: Planted Rejuvenation
LCH-5_2_6_1.tip: Forest renewal started by people, who deliberately plant young trees or sow seeds, e.g. replanting saplings after a harvest.

LCH-5_2_6_2.label: Natural Forest Succession
LCH-5_2_6_2.tip: Forest renewal that happens naturally, with trees reproducing from their own seeds and fruits and no human planting involved.

LCH-5_2_6_2_1.label: Self-Seeded Forest Succession
LCH-5_2_6_2_1.tip: Natural forest regrowth where trees spread by dropping or scattering their own seeds, e.g. birch seedlings appearing in a clearing.

LCH-5_2_6_2_2.label: Re-Sprouting Forest
LCH-5_2_6_2_2.tip: Natural regrowth of new shoots from roots, branches or a cut or broken stump, e.g. after coppicing.

LCH-5_2_7.label: Silvicultural Measure
LCH-5_2_7.tip: Groups care measures applied to forest trees and soil to keep them healthy and growing well, such as thinning, pruning or drainage.

LCH-5_2_7_1.label: Forest Cleaning, Weeding
LCH-5_2_7_1.tip: Clearing competing plants such as weeds or unwanted young trees from around seedlings during the first years of a new forest.

LCH-5_2_7_2.label: Forest Thinning
LCH-5_2_7_2.tip: Removing some trees from a stand so the best ones get more light, water, nutrients and space to grow.

LCH-5_2_7_3.label: Forest Pruning
LCH-5_2_7_3.tip: Selectively cutting off parts of trees, such as branches, buds or roots, to shape growth or remove dead or damaged parts.

LCH-5_2_7_4.label: Ring-Barking, Girdling
LCH-5_2_7_4.tip: Cutting a ring of bark around a tree's trunk, which interrupts its flow of nutrients and causes it to die gradually.

LCH-5_2_7_5.label: Interplanting
LCH-5_2_7_5.tip: Planting young trees of other species within a single-species forest to make it more mixed, e.g. adding beech to a pine plantation.

LCH-5_2_7_6.label: Dead Wood Removal
LCH-5_2_7_6.tip: Clearing fallen or standing dead trees and branches out of a forest.

LCH-5_2_7_7.label: Forest Irrigation
LCH-5_2_7_7.tip: Watering forest trees artificially, e.g. to help young plantations through dry periods.

LCH-5_2_7_8.label: Forest Drainage
LCH-5_2_7_8.tip: Draining wet forest land with ditches or pipes so that trees can grow better.

LCH-5_2_7_9.label: Forest Liming
LCH-5_2_7_9.tip: Spreading lime on forest soil to reduce its acidity, e.g. in areas affected by acid rain.

LCH-5_2_7_10.label: Forest Firebreak
LCH-5_2_7_10.tip: A strip cleared of trees and burnable vegetation inside or around a forest, meant to stop or slow the spread of wildfires.

LCH-5_2_8.label: Silvicultural Harvest and Regeneration Method
LCH-5_2_8.tip: Groups the common methods of harvesting timber, which in forestry are closely tied to how the forest is then regenerated.

LCH-5_2_8_1.label: Clearcutting
LCH-5_2_8_1.tip: Felling all trees on a plot at once, leaving none standing, e.g. a fully harvested section of plantation awaiting replanting.

LCH-5_2_8_2.label: Shelterwood Cutting
LCH-5_2_8_2.tip: Felling mature trees gradually, a few at a time and spread evenly across the plot, so the remaining trees shelter the young growth.

LCH-5_2_8_3.label: Femel Cutting
LCH-5_2_8_3.tip: Felling mature trees over several years in scattered groups or patches, creating island-like gaps where new trees grow.

LCH-5_2_8_4.label: Strip Cutting
LCH-5_2_8_4.tip: Felling a mature forest step by step in strips, starting at the outer edge of the plot and moving inward year by year.

LCH-5_2_8_5.label: Selection Cutting
LCH-5_2_8_5.tip: Harvesting only selected trees that are ready for cutting while leaving the rest to keep growing, which keeps the forest continuously covered.

LCH-5_2_8_6.label: Coppicing
LCH-5_2_8_6.tip: Repeatedly cutting tree stems close to the ground so new shoots grow from the stump, which are harvested again in later cycles.

LCH-5_2_8_7.label: Pollarding
LCH-5_2_8_7.tip: Cutting a tree's top a few metres above ground so it sprouts many thin shoots, e.g. for leafy fodder or neatly shaped street trees.

LCH-5_2_9.label: Forest Product Type
LCH-5_2_9.tip: Groups forests by what their trees are used for: wood, fibre, energy or non-wood products such as cork or resin.

LCH-5_2_9_1.label: Wood Product
LCH-5_2_9_1.tip: Forests whose main product is wood itself, whether for building material, fuel or fibre for paper.

LCH-5_2_9_1_1.label: Timber Wood
LCH-5_2_9_1_1.tip: Wood harvested for use as construction material, e.g. for furniture, buildings or bridges.

LCH-5_2_9_1_2.label: Energy Wood
LCH-5_2_9_1_2.tip: Wood harvested to be burned for energy or turned into charcoal, e.g. firewood.

LCH-5_2_9_1_3.label: Wood Fibre
LCH-5_2_9_1_3.tip: Wood harvested to produce cellulose, the raw material for pulp and paper.

LCH-5_2_9_2.label: Non-Wood Product
LCH-5_2_9_2.tip: Goods from forests that are of biological origin but are not wood, e.g. cork, resin, rubber, bamboo or Christmas trees.

LCH-5_2_9_2_1.label: Cork
LCH-5_2_9_2_1.tip: Bark harvested from cork oak trees, used for products such as wine stoppers and insulation boards.

LCH-5_2_9_2_2.label: Resin
LCH-5_2_9_2_2.tip: Sticky sap collected by tapping a hole into a tree trunk and gathering the resin the tree produces to seal the wound.

LCH-5_2_9_2_3.label: Latex, Natural Rubber
LCH-5_2_9_2_3.tip: Milky sap gathered from wounds in the bark of rubber trees, mostly grown on tropical plantations, and used to make natural rubber.

LCH-5_2_9_2_4.label: Incense
LCH-5_2_9_2_4.tip: Aromatic resin from Boswellia trees, burnt to give off fragrant smoke in religious or ritual ceremonies.

LCH-5_2_9_2_5.label: Myrrh
LCH-5_2_9_2_5.tip: Gum-resin from small thorny Commiphora trees, used over the centuries as perfume, incense and medicine.

LCH-5_2_10.label: Forest History Type
LCH-5_2_10.tip: Groups forests by their origin and past: untouched primary forest, naturally regrown forest, or forest planted by people.

LCH-5_2_10_1.label: Primary or Virgin Forest
LCH-5_2_10_1.tip: Forest of native trees that regenerated naturally and shows no clearly visible signs of human activity, e.g. untouched old-growth woodland.

LCH-5_2_10_2.label: Secondary or Naturally Regenerated Forest
LCH-5_2_10_2.tip: Forest that regrew naturally but shows clear signs of past human activity, e.g. after selective logging, farming or human-caused fires.

LCH-5_2_10_3.label: Reforestation
LCH-5_2_10_3.tip: Re-establishing forest by planting or sowing on land already used as forest, e.g. replanting seedlings after a clear cut or storm damage.

LCH-5_2_10_4.label: Afforestation
LCH-5_2_10_4.tip: Creating new forest by planting or sowing trees on land that was not forest before, e.g. on former farmland or grassland.

LCH-5_2_11.label: Forest Tree Species
LCH-5_2_11.tip: Groups forests by the main tree types growing there, listed by their scientific genus name, such as Quercus (oaks) or Pinus (pines).

LCH-5_2_11_1.label: Abies
LCH-5_2_11_1.tip: Firs, evergreen conifers with flat needles and upright cones, e.g. the silver fir.

LCH-5_2_11_2.label: Acer
LCH-5_2_11_2.tip: Maples, broadleaved trees known for their lobed leaves and winged seeds, e.g. the sycamore maple.

LCH-5_2_11_3.label: Aesculus
LCH-5_2_11_3.tip: Horse chestnuts, broadleaved trees with large hand-shaped leaves and shiny brown conkers.

LCH-5_2_11_4.label: Alnus
LCH-5_2_11_4.tip: Alders, broadleaved trees often found along rivers and in wet ground, e.g. the black alder.

LCH-5_2_11_5.label: Betula
LCH-5_2_11_5.tip: Birches, broadleaved trees often recognised by their pale, peeling bark, e.g. the silver birch.

LCH-5_2_11_6.label: Carpinus
LCH-5_2_11_6.tip: Hornbeams, broadleaved trees with very hard wood, often found in mixed woods and hedges.

LCH-5_2_11_7.label: Castanea
LCH-5_2_11_7.tip: Sweet chestnuts, broadleaved trees grown for their edible nuts and durable wood.

LCH-5_2_11_8.label: Cedrus
LCH-5_2_11_8.tip: Cedars, large evergreen conifers with needles in clusters, e.g. the cedar of Lebanon.

LCH-5_2_11_9.label: Corylus
LCH-5_2_11_9.tip: Hazels, small broadleaved trees or shrubs that produce hazelnuts, often coppiced.

LCH-5_2_11_10.label: Cupressoideae
LCH-5_2_11_10.tip: Trees of the cypress family, evergreen conifers with scale-like leaves, e.g. cypresses and junipers.

LCH-5_2_11_11.label: Eucalyptus
LCH-5_2_11_11.tip: Eucalyptus or gum trees, fast-growing evergreen broadleaved trees originally from Australia and often grown in plantations.

LCH-5_2_11_12.label: Fagus
LCH-5_2_11_12.tip: Beeches, broadleaved trees with smooth grey bark that often form dense forests, e.g. the European beech.

LCH-5_2_11_13.label: Fraxinus
LCH-5_2_11_13.tip: Ash trees, broadleaved trees with feathery compound leaves, e.g. the common ash.

LCH-5_2_11_14.label: Ginkgo
LCH-5_2_11_14.tip: Ginkgo, an ancient tree species with fan-shaped leaves, often planted in parks and along streets.

LCH-5_2_11_15.label: Juglans
LCH-5_2_11_15.tip: Walnut trees, broadleaved trees grown for their nuts and valuable timber.

LCH-5_2_11_16.label: Larix
LCH-5_2_11_16.tip: Larches, conifers that unusually shed their needles in autumn, e.g. the European larch.

LCH-5_2_11_17.label: Picea
LCH-5_2_11_17.tip: Spruces, evergreen conifers with short needles and hanging cones, e.g. the Norway spruce.

LCH-5_2_11_18.label: Pinus
LCH-5_2_11_18.tip: Pines, evergreen conifers with long needles in bundles, e.g. the Scots pine.

LCH-5_2_11_19.label: Platanus
LCH-5_2_11_19.tip: Plane trees, large broadleaved trees with flaking patchy bark, common along city streets.

LCH-5_2_11_20.label: Populus
LCH-5_2_11_20.tip: Poplars, fast-growing broadleaved trees, including aspens, often planted for wood or along roads.

LCH-5_2_11_21.label: Pseudotsuga
LCH-5_2_11_21.tip: Douglas firs, tall fast-growing conifers originally from North America and widely planted for timber.

LCH-5_2_11_22.label: Quercus
LCH-5_2_11_22.tip: Oaks, long-lived broadleaved trees that bear acorns, e.g. the pedunculate or cork oak.

LCH-5_2_11_23.label: Salix
LCH-5_2_11_23.tip: Willows, broadleaved trees and shrubs usually growing in wet places, also grown as short-rotation energy crops.

LCH-5_2_11_24.label: Taxus
LCH-5_2_11_24.tip: Yews, slow-growing evergreen conifers with dark needles and red berry-like fruits.

LCH-5_2_11_25.label: Tilia
LCH-5_2_11_25.tip: Lime or linden trees, broadleaved trees with heart-shaped leaves and fragrant flowers.

LCH-5_2_11_26.label: Ulmus
LCH-5_2_11_26.tip: Elms, broadleaved trees with rough, uneven leaves, many of which were hit hard by Dutch elm disease.

LCH-5_3.label: Industrial Land Management
LCH-5_3.tip: Groups characteristics of land used for industry, mainly how mining is done and which raw materials are extracted.

LCH-5_3_1.label: Mining Technique
LCH-5_3_1.tip: Groups the methods used to extract raw materials from the ground, such as open pits, underground mines or fracking.

LCH-5_3_1_1.label: Surface Open Pit Mining
LCH-5_3_1_1.tip: Extracting materials from a large open hole dug down from the surface, e.g. an open-cast coal mine or quarry.

LCH-5_3_1_2.label: Underground Mining
LCH-5_3_1_2.tip: Extracting materials through tunnels and shafts below the surface, e.g. a deep coal or metal mine.

LCH-5_3_1_3.label: Under Water Mining
LCH-5_3_1_3.tip: Extracting materials from beneath water, e.g. dredging sand and gravel from a lake or riverbed.

LCH-5_3_1_4.label: Salines Extraction Site
LCH-5_3_1_4.tip: A site where salt is won from salt water, e.g. shallow evaporation ponds along a coast.

LCH-5_3_1_5.label: Leaching, Solution Mining
LCH-5_3_1_5.tip: Extracting minerals by dissolving them with liquids pumped into the ground or poured over ore, then collecting the solution, e.g. some salt or uranium mining.

LCH-5_3_1_6.label: Fracking
LCH-5_3_1_6.tip: Releasing oil or gas from deep rock by pumping in fluid under high pressure to crack it open.

LCH-5_3_2.label: Mining Product Type
LCH-5_3_2.tip: Groups the kinds of raw materials taken from mines and extraction sites, from fuels such as coal to metal ores and stone.

LCH-5_3_2_1.label: Fossil Hydrocarbon Fuels
LCH-5_3_2_1.tip: Fuels formed from ancient plant and animal remains, extracted from the ground, e.g. coal, crude oil or natural gas.

LCH-5_3_2_1_1.label: Hard Coal
LCH-5_3_2_1_1.tip: Hard, black, high-energy coal, usually mined deep underground and used for power and steel making.

LCH-5_3_2_1_2.label: Coal Lignite
LCH-5_3_2_1_2.tip: Lignite or brown coal, a soft, lower-grade coal often dug from large open-cast mines.

LCH-5_3_2_1_3.label: Peat
LCH-5_3_2_1_3.tip: Partly decayed plant material from bogs, dug up and dried for fuel or garden use.

LCH-5_3_2_1_4.label: Crude Oil
LCH-5_3_2_1_4.tip: Petroleum pumped from underground reservoirs in its raw, unrefined form, e.g. from oil wells.

LCH-5_3_2_1_5.label: Oil Sands
LCH-5_3_2_1_5.tip: Sand or sandstone soaked with a thick, tar-like oil, mined and processed to obtain petroleum.

LCH-5_3_2_1_6.label: Bituminous Rocks
LCH-5_3_2_1_6.tip: Rocks containing bitumen or oil-rich material, e.g. oil shale, mined as a source of fuel.

LCH-5_3_2_1_7.label: Mineral Gas
LCH-5_3_2_1_7.tip: Natural gas extracted from underground deposits, mainly used for heating and generating power.

LCH-5_3_2_2.label: Metal Ores
LCH-5_3_2_2.tip: Rocks mined because they contain metals worth extracting, e.g. iron, copper or rare earth ores.

LCH-5_3_2_2_1.label: Iron Ores
LCH-5_3_2_2_1.tip: Rock rich in iron, mined as the raw material for making iron and steel.

LCH-5_3_2_2_2.label: Nonferrous Metal Ores
LCH-5_3_2_2_2.tip: Ores of metals other than iron, e.g. copper, zinc, lead, aluminium or gold.

LCH-5_3_2_2_3.label: Rare Earths
LCH-5_3_2_2_3.tip: Ores of a group of special metals used in electronics, magnets and batteries, e.g. neodymium.

LCH-5_3_2_3.label: Non-Metallic Minerals
LCH-5_3_2_3.tip: Minerals extracted for uses other than metal, e.g. building stone, gravel, salt or gemstones.

LCH-5_3_2_3_1.label: Stones and Earths
LCH-5_3_2_3_1.tip: Rock, sand, gravel, clay and similar materials dug up mainly for building and construction, e.g. from a gravel pit or quarry.

LCH-5_3_2_3_2.label: Chemical Minerals
LCH-5_3_2_3_2.tip: Minerals mined as raw materials for the chemical or fertiliser industries, e.g. potash or salt.

LCH-5_3_2_3_2_1.label: Salt
LCH-5_3_2_3_2_1.tip: Rock salt or sea salt extracted from mines, brine or evaporation ponds, used in food, industry and road gritting.

LCH-5_3_2_3_3.label: Precious And Semi-Precious Stones
LCH-5_3_2_3_3.tip: Gemstones mined for jewellery or decoration, e.g. diamonds, rubies or amethysts.

LCH-5_3_2_4.label: Other Mining Material
LCH-5_3_2_4.tip: Mined or extracted materials that do not fit in the other product groups listed here.

LCH-5_4.label: Terrain Modification and Land Engineering Measure
LCH-5_4.tip: Groups ways in which people reshape the ground or install structures on it, e.g. terraces, levelled ski slopes or avalanche barriers.

LCH-5_4_1.label: Terraced Terrain
LCH-5_4_1.tip: Slopes reshaped into a series of level steps, mostly so they can be farmed, e.g. vineyard or rice terraces on a hillside.

LCH-5_4_2.label: Artificial Terrain Modification
LCH-5_4_2.tip: Ground heavily reshaped by earthworks, e.g. steep land levelled out or slopes sculpted for ski pistes.

LCH-5_4_3.label: Artificial Snow Preparation
LCH-5_4_3.tip: Land, usually ski pistes, covered with man-made snow from snow cannons to improve skiing and extend the season.

LCH-5_4_4.label: Snow Farming Area
LCH-5_4_4.tip: Areas where snow is collected in winter and covered with insulating material so it lasts through the summer, e.g. for ski slopes next season.

LCH-5_4_5.label: Avalanche Prevention or Protection Installation
LCH-5_4_5.tip: Structures that stop avalanches from starting or protect areas against them, e.g. snow fences or barriers on mountain slopes.

LCH-5_5.label: Administrative Regulations, Use Constraints
LCH-5_5.tip: Groups legal rules and restrictions on how land may be used or entered, such as protected areas and access limits.

LCH-5_5_1.label: Access Restriction
LCH-5_5_1.tip: Groups land by who is allowed to enter it, from open public access to military-only zones.

LCH-5_5_1_1.label: Civil, Open
LCH-5_5_1_1.tip: Land open to the general public, where anyone may enter, e.g. a public park or common land.

LCH-5_5_1_2.label: Civil and Military
LCH-5_5_1_2.tip: Land that both civilians and the military may use and enter, e.g. a shared training ground with public paths.

LCH-5_5_1_3.label: Temporary Restricted
LCH-5_5_1_3.tip: Land closed to access for a limited time, e.g. after a severe natural disaster or a contamination event.

LCH-5_5_1_4.label: Military Only, Restricted
LCH-5_5_1_4.tip: Land only the military may enter, with others kept out or allowed in only by special permission, e.g. a military base.

LCH-5_5_2.label: Protected Area Type
LCH-5_5_2.tip: Groups the kinds of legal protection status an area can have, e.g. nature reserves, national parks or Natura 2000 sites.

LCH-5_5_2_1.label: Nature Conservation Area
LCH-5_5_2_1.tip: Land under strict legal nature protection, where many activities such as farming, building or lighting fires are forbidden.

LCH-5_5_2_2.label: Landscape Conservation Area
LCH-5_5_2_2.tip: Protected land where activities like farming and forestry are allowed to a degree, but the look of the landscape must be preserved.

LCH-5_5_2_3.label: Natura2000
LCH-5_5_2_3.tip: Areas listed under European law as part of the Natura 2000 network of protected sites for nature.

LCH-5_5_2_4.label: Birds Retrieval Area
LCH-5_5_2_4.tip: Areas with strict access limits to protect birds, either all year or during the breeding season.

LCH-5_5_2_5.label: Biosphere Reserve
LCH-5_5_2_5.tip: Areas designated by UNESCO to manage nature and human culture together, often with a strictly protected core and less restricted outer zones.

LCH-5_5_2_6.label: Geopark
LCH-5_5_2_6.tip: UNESCO-designated areas with internationally important geology, managed for protection, education and sustainable development.

LCH-5_5_2_7.label: National Park
LCH-5_5_2_7.tip: A larger area run by an authority mainly to conserve nature, often combined with recreation and visitor facilities.

LCH-5_5_2_8.label: Other Protected Area Type
LCH-5_5_2_8.tip: Protected areas with a legal status not covered by the other types listed here.

LCH-6.label: Status, Condition
LCH-6.tip: Groups characteristics describing the current state or condition of a piece of land and, if it is damaged, the reason why.

LCH-6_1.label: Land Use Status
LCH-6_1.tip: Groups labels describing the state a piece of land is in regarding its use, e.g. under construction, out of use or abandoned.

LCH-6_1_1.label: Under Construction
LCH-6_1_1.tip: Land being turned into man-made surfaces, e.g. a building site with excavations or earthworks whose final use is already decided.

LCH-6_1_2.label: Never Been in Use
LCH-6_1_2.tip: Land that is not used and shows no recognisable traces of ever having been used by people.

LCH-6_1_3.label: Out of Use
LCH-6_1_3.tip: Land that is temporarily not used but will probably be used again, e.g. a factory site on hold.

LCH-6_1_4.label: Abandoned
LCH-6_1_4.tip: Land no longer in use that cannot serve its original purpose without major repair, e.g. a derelict industrial site.

LCH-6_1_5.label: Clear Cut
LCH-6_1_5.tip: Land from which trees or shrubs have recently been removed, e.g. a freshly felled forest plot.

LCH-6_1_6.label: Collapsed, Destroyed, Damaged
LCH-6_1_6.tip: Marks objects that are no longer intact or usable because they were destroyed or collapsed, mostly buildings, structures or utilities, e.g. a building left in ruins.

LCH-6_1_7.label: Managed Nature Restoration
LCH-6_1_7.tip: Areas being deliberately returned to a natural or semi-natural state, e.g. by removing paving, cleaning up polluted ground, sowing plants or restoring natural soil moisture.

LCH-6_2.label: Damage Reason
LCH-6_2.tip: Groups the possible causes of damage to an area, from natural hazards such as floods or earthquakes to human-made harm such as pollution or demolition.

LCH-6_2_1.label: Geological Or Hydrological
LCH-6_2_1.tip: Damage caused by processes of the solid earth or of water, e.g. earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, landslides or floods.

LCH-6_2_1_1.label: Tsunami
LCH-6_2_1_1.tip: Damage from a long, powerful wave in the sea or a large lake that reaches land, e.g. one set off by an undersea earthquake or a landslide into a lake.

LCH-6_2_1_2.label: Volcanic Eruption
LCH-6_2_1_2.tip: Damage from a volcano releasing hot magma, ash and gases, including directly linked effects such as ash fall, explosions and fast-moving hot volcanic flows.

LCH-6_2_1_3.label: Earthquake
LCH-6_2_1_3.tip: Damage from ground shaking when stress in the Earth's crust is suddenly released, along with direct effects such as soil turning soft and losing strength.

LCH-6_2_1_4.label: Subsidence and Collapse
LCH-6_2_1_4.tip: Damage from the ground sinking or caving in, mainly downward movement when weathered or compacted rock or soil can no longer carry its own weight.

LCH-6_2_1_5.label: Landslide
LCH-6_2_1_5.tip: Damage from soil, rock and other material moving downhill when a slope fails, e.g. slides, rock falls or debris flows.

LCH-6_2_1_6.label: Snow Avalanche
LCH-6_2_1_6.tip: Damage from a large mass of snow sliding rapidly down a slope, often carrying trees and rocks along its path.

LCH-6_2_1_7.label: Flood
LCH-6_2_1_7.tip: Damage from water covering land that is normally dry, e.g. a river overflowing its banks, a flash flood or a tidal flood.

LCH-6_2_2.label: Meteorological Or Climatological
LCH-6_2_2.tip: Groups damage caused by weather or by longer-term climate conditions, e.g. droughts, heat waves, storms or lightning.

LCH-6_2_2_1.label: Drought
LCH-6_2_2_1.tip: Damage from a long, widespread period with less water than usual due to climate variability; not the same as a naturally dry climate.

LCH-6_2_2_2.label: Extreme Temperatures
LCH-6_2_2_2.tip: Damage from unusually hot or cold spells lasting longer than normal, e.g. heat waves or cold waves with frost.

LCH-6_2_2_3.label: Storm Damage
LCH-6_2_2_3.tip: Damage from violent, high-speed winds such as tornadoes or hurricanes, e.g. trees blown over in a forest.

LCH-6_2_2_4.label: Lightning
LCH-6_2_2_4.tip: Damage from lightning strikes, the electrical discharges usually linked to thunderclouds but which can also happen in dry conditions.

LCH-6_2_2_5.label: Storm Surge
LCH-6_2_2_5.tip: Damage from seawater pushed onto land by a storm or a sudden change in air pressure, e.g. during a hurricane; treated separately from other floods.

LCH-6_2_3.label: Fire
LCH-6_2_3.tip: Groups damage caused by fire breaking out and spreading, whether above ground in vegetation or below the surface.

LCH-6_2_3_1.label: Forest Fire, Wildfire
LCH-6_2_3_1.tip: Damage from fire spreading over vegetated land, such as forests and other wooded land, e.g. a summer wildfire; planned controlled burns are excluded.

LCH-6_2_3_2.label: Underground Fire
LCH-6_2_3_2.tip: Damage from fire burning below the ground surface, typically in soils rich in peat or coal, e.g. a smouldering peat fire.

LCH-6_2_4.label: Biological
LCH-6_2_4.tip: Groups damage caused by living organisms or what they produce, e.g. insect pests, diseases or grazing animals.

LCH-6_2_4_1.label: Insect Infestation
LCH-6_2_4_1.tip: Damage caused by large numbers of insects attacking plants or trees, e.g. bark beetles killing patches of forest.

LCH-6_2_4_2.label: Mould Infestation
LCH-6_2_4_2.tip: Damage caused by mould or similar fungi spreading on plants, materials or buildings.

LCH-6_2_4_3.label: Epidemic
LCH-6_2_4_3.tip: Harm from a disease outbreak that spreads quickly among people, animals or plants in an area.

LCH-6_2_4_4.label: Allergens
LCH-6_2_4_4.tip: Biological substances, such as pollen, that can cause allergic reactions in many people in an area.

LCH-6_2_4_5.label: Animal Browsing, Overgrazing
LCH-6_2_4_5.tip: Vegetation damaged by animals biting off plant parts or grazing so heavily, even tearing out roots, that plants cannot recover.

LCH-6_2_4_6.label: Animal Trampling
LCH-6_2_4_6.tip: Damage to plant cover caused by animals repeatedly walking over it, e.g. bare paths worn by livestock.

LCH-6_2_5.label: Cosmic
LCH-6_2_5.tip: Groups damage that originates from outer space, such as meteorite impacts or radiation.

LCH-6_2_5_1.label: Meteorite Impact
LCH-6_2_5_1.tip: Damage caused by solid material from outer space striking the Earth's surface, e.g. a crater left by a meteorite.

LCH-6_2_5_2.label: Magnetic Disruption
LCH-6_2_5_2.tip: Damage linked to disturbances of the Earth's magnetic field caused from space, e.g. during strong solar storms.

LCH-6_2_5_3.label: Solar and Cosmic Radiation
LCH-6_2_5_3.tip: Damage from radiation coming from outer space, such as ultraviolet light or gamma rays.

LCH-6_2_6.label: Contamination Or Pollution
LCH-6_2_6.tip: Groups damage caused by harmful substances in the ground, water or air, e.g. chemicals, oil, radioactivity or plastic.

LCH-6_2_6_1.label: Radioactive Contamination
LCH-6_2_6_1.tip: Land or water polluted by radioactive material, e.g. areas affected by a nuclear accident.

LCH-6_2_6_2.label: Chemical, Toxic Pollution
LCH-6_2_6_2.tip: Land or water polluted by harmful chemicals or toxic substances, e.g. waste from industrial sites.

LCH-6_2_6_3.label: Soil Salinization
LCH-6_2_6_3.tip: Soil damaged by a build-up of salts, which harms plant growth and can make farmland less productive.

LCH-6_2_6_4.label: Oil contaminated
LCH-6_2_6_4.tip: Land or water polluted by oil, e.g. after a pipeline leak or an oil spill on a coast.

LCH-6_2_6_5.label: Explosives Contamination
LCH-6_2_6_5.tip: Areas contaminated by military ammunition or industrial explosives, e.g. a former firing range with unexploded shells.

LCH-6_2_6_6.label: Plastic pollution
LCH-6_2_6_6.tip: Areas polluted by plastic, whether large pieces of litter or tiny microplastic particles.

LCH-6_2_7.label: Intentional Or Accidental Structural Damage
LCH-6_2_7.tip: Groups damage to buildings and other structures caused by people, either on purpose or by accident, e.g. demolition or neglect.

LCH-6_2_7_1.label: Structural Decay
LCH-6_2_7_1.tip: Damage from structures slowly falling apart over time, e.g. an abandoned building crumbling through lack of maintenance.

LCH-6_2_7_2.label: Demolition, Explosion
LCH-6_2_7_2.tip: Damage from structures being deliberately torn down or blown up, or from an explosion.

LCH-6_3.label: Degenerative Process
LCH-6_3.tip: Groups slow processes that wear down or degrade land over time, e.g. soil erosion, desertification or melting glaciers.

LCH-6_3_1.label: Deforestation
LCH-6_3_1.tip: Loss of tree cover, whether from natural causes or human activity, e.g. drought, storms, clear-cutting or soil erosion.

LCH-6_3_2.label: Soil Erosion
LCH-6_3_2.tip: Loss of fertile topsoil carried away by wind, flowing water or gravity, e.g. soil washed off a field after heavy rain.

LCH-6_3_3.label: Desertification
LCH-6_3_3.tip: Vegetated land gradually turning into desert, typically after years of low rainfall combined with human or animal pressure such as soil salinization.

LCH-6_3_4.label: Glacier Melting
LCH-6_3_4.tip: Areas where glaciers have shrunk in size or thickness by melting as average temperatures rise.

LCH-7.label: Geographical Characteristics
LCH-7.tip: Groups characteristics describing where a piece of land lies geographically, e.g. its habitat, altitude zone, climate, landscape setting and terrain.

LCH-7_1.label: Habitat Context
LCH-7_1.tip: Groups types of natural or human-shaped surroundings in which people, animals and plants live, largely following the European EUNIS habitat types.

LCH-7_1_1.label: Marine Habitats
LCH-7_1_1.tip: Habitats in the sea, from shallow coastal waters to the deep ocean floor, e.g. seagrass meadows or reefs.

LCH-7_1_2.label: Coastal Habitats
LCH-7_1_2.tip: Habitats along the coast where land meets sea, e.g. beaches, dunes, sea cliffs and shingle shores.

LCH-7_1_3.label: Inland Surface Waters Habitats
LCH-7_1_3.tip: Habitats in and around freshwater on land, e.g. lakes, ponds, rivers and streams.

LCH-7_1_4.label: Mires, Bogs and Fens
LCH-7_1_4.tip: Wet habitats with waterlogged, often peaty ground, e.g. raised bogs or fens fed by groundwater.

LCH-7_1_5.label: Grasslands and Lands Dominated By Forbs, Mosses Or Lichens
LCH-7_1_5.tip: Open habitats where grasses, herbs, mosses or lichens dominate rather than trees or shrubs, e.g. meadows and pastures.

LCH-7_1_6.label: Heathland, Scrub and Tundra
LCH-7_1_6.tip: Habitats dominated by low woody plants or cold-adapted vegetation, e.g. heather moors, shrubland or Arctic tundra.

LCH-7_1_7.label: Woodland, Forest and Other Wooded Land
LCH-7_1_7.tip: Habitats dominated by trees, from dense forests to more open wooded land, e.g. beech forests or pine woodland.

LCH-7_1_8.label: Inland Unvegetated Or Sparsely Vegetated Habitats
LCH-7_1_8.tip: Inland habitats with bare or very sparse plant cover, e.g. rock outcrops, screes, sand areas or snowfields.

LCH-7_1_9.label: Regularly Or Recently Cultivated Agricultural, Horticultural and Domestic Habitats
LCH-7_1_9.tip: Habitats created and kept up by farming, gardening or domestic use, e.g. arable fields, orchards or gardens.

LCH-7_1_10.label: Constructed, Industrial and Other Artificial Habitats
LCH-7_1_10.tip: Habitats made or heavily shaped by human construction and industry, e.g. buildings, roads, quarries or waste tips.

LCH-7_1_11.label: Habitat Complexes
LCH-7_1_11.tip: Areas made up of several different habitat types closely mixed together and treated as one unit, e.g. a river delta.

LCH-7_1_12.label: Lagoon
LCH-7_1_12.tip: Shallow coastal body of water separated from the sea by a barrier such as a sandbar, often with brackish water.

LCH-7_1_13.label: Estuary
LCH-7_1_13.tip: The wide mouth of a river where freshwater mixes with seawater and tides reach inland.

LCH-7_1_14.label: Marine Inlet, Fjord
LCH-7_1_14.tip: A narrow arm of the sea reaching into the land, e.g. a long, steep-sided fjord carved by glaciers.

LCH-7_1_15.label: Coastal Salt Marsh
LCH-7_1_15.tip: Low coastal land covered by salt-tolerant plants and regularly flooded by seawater at high tide.

LCH-7_1_16.label: Intertidal Flat
LCH-7_1_16.tip: Flat stretches of mud or sand that are covered by the sea at high tide and exposed at low tide, e.g. mudflats.

LCH-7_2.label: Height Zone
LCH-7_2.tip: Groups altitude bands in mountain regions, where temperature, moisture and vegetation change step by step as height increases.

LCH-7_2_1.label: Planar Zone
LCH-7_2_1.tip: Lowland of flat, plain areas with the usual temperatures of the local climate; ideal ground for farming and settlements.

LCH-7_2_2.label: Collin Zone
LCH-7_2_2.tip: Hilly land with gently rolling terrain, usually forming the upper limit for vineyards; also called the colline zone.

LCH-7_2_3.label: Submontane Zone
LCH-7_2_3.tip: Zone with more pronounced relief, valleys and mid-height peaks, where growing crops is rare if it happens at all.

LCH-7_2_4.label: Montane Zone
LCH-7_2_4.tip: Clearly cooler zone at the peaks of middle mountain ranges, forming the transition towards the high mountains.

LCH-7_2_5.label: High Montane Zone
LCH-7_2_5.tip: Upper limit of broadleaved forest where conifers dominate; places here are only inhabited seasonally.

LCH-7_2_6.label: Subalpine Zone
LCH-7_2_6.tip: Transition zone at the upper edge of forests, where scattered trees give way to dwarf pines.

LCH-7_2_7.label: Alpine Zone
LCH-7_2_7.tip: Zone between the tree line and the snow line, where vegetation is limited to low herbs, grasses and dwarf shrubs, e.g. alpine meadows.

LCH-7_2_8.label: Nival Zone
LCH-7_2_8.tip: Highest altitude zone, covered by snow or ice for all or most of the year, where glaciers form and plants are essentially absent.

LCH-7_3.label: Geographical Context
LCH-7_3.tip: Groups descriptions of the wider setting a piece of land sits in, e.g. urban, rural, coastal or mountain surroundings, whose borders are often fuzzy.

LCH-7_3_1.label: Inland Context
LCH-7_3_1.tip: Land far enough from the coast that it is no longer directly influenced by the sea; the opposite of a coastal setting.

LCH-7_3_2.label: Coastal Context
LCH-7_3_2.tip: Land close to the seashore, where nearness to the sea shapes things like ports, towns, industry and tourism.

LCH-7_3_3.label: Island Context
LCH-7_3_3.tip: Land on an island, influenced by the surrounding sea and by its transport links to the mainland; an island can itself have inland and coastal parts.

LCH-7_3_4.label: Oceanic Context
LCH-7_3_4.tip: Open sea far from any coastline, from the edge of the continental shelf out to deep-sea areas.

LCH-7_3_5.label: Urban Context
LCH-7_3_5.tip: Setting of cities and their suburbs, where built-up areas and transport networks dominate the landscape and many people live.

LCH-7_3_6.label: Rural Context
LCH-7_3_6.tip: Countryside dominated by farmland or forest, where villages exist but large cities are absent and population density is medium to low.

LCH-7_3_7.label: Riparian Context
LCH-7_3_7.tip: Land along riverbanks, generally flat and exposed to changing water levels and floods, often with moisture-loving plants such as willows.

LCH-7_3_8.label: Mountain Context
LCH-7_3_8.tip: Land shaped by mountains, including the valleys between them, with steep terrain and several climate and vegetation zones.

LCH-7_4.label: Geomorphological Landform Type
LCH-7_4.tip: Groups the shape of the land surface, e.g. a valley, dune or plateau; currently a placeholder where the landform is written as free text.

LCH-7_4_1.label: Geomorphological Landform
LCH-7_4_1.tip: A free-text note naming the landform found at a place, e.g. 'moraine' or 'river terrace', since no fixed list of landforms exists yet.

LCH-7_5.label: Littoral Zone
LCH-7_5.tip: Groups the bands along a shoreline, at the sea, a lake or a river, sorted by how often they are under water.

LCH-7_5_1.label: Epilittoral
LCH-7_5_1.tip: Strip above the shoreline that water does not reach directly; only high groundwater and moist, sometimes salty soil affect it, plus rare extreme storm surges.

LCH-7_5_2.label: Supralittoral
LCH-7_5_2.tip: Splash and spray zone just above the waterline, rarely covered by water but wetted by spray from waves; flooded only during storms or floods.

LCH-7_5_3.label: Eulittoral, Intertidal
LCH-7_5_3.tip: Zone between low and high water, regularly covered and uncovered by tides on coasts or by changing water levels along rivers and lakes.

LCH-7_5_4.label: Infralittoral, Sublittoral
LCH-7_5_4.tip: Zone below the low-water line that is normally always under water, on coasts as well as in rivers and lakes; also called subtidal.

LCH-7_6.label: Physical Climate Zone
LCH-7_6.tip: Groups broad climate zones of the world, useful e.g. for noting which climate a crop or plant type naturally belongs to.

LCH-7_6_1.label: Tropical Climate Zone
LCH-7_6_1.tip: Warm climate zone near the equator, hot all year round, e.g. where rainforests or banana plantations are found.

LCH-7_6_2.label: Subtropical Climate Zone
LCH-7_6_2.tip: Climate zone between the tropics and the temperate zone, with hot summers and mild winters, e.g. around the Mediterranean.

LCH-7_6_3.label: Temperate Climate Zone
LCH-7_6_3.tip: Climate zone of moderate temperatures with clear seasons, such as most of central and western Europe.

LCH-7_6_4.label: Polar and Subpolar Climate Zone
LCH-7_6_4.tip: Cold climate zone near and around the poles, with long winters and short, cool summers, e.g. the Arctic.

LCH-7_7.label: Terrain Characteristics
LCH-7_7.tip: Groups measurable properties of the ground surface's shape, such as its height, steepness and the direction it faces.

LCH-7_7_1.label: Terrain Parameters
LCH-7_7_1.tip: Groups measured values describing terrain at a point, namely elevation, slope and aspect, usually stored as grid (raster) data.

LCH-7_7_1_1.label: Terrain Elevation
LCH-7_7_1_1.tip: Height of the ground above sea level, measured in meters.

LCH-7_7_1_2.label: Terrain Slope
LCH-7_7_1_2.tip: How steep the ground rises, i.e. the slope angle, recorded in degrees.

LCH-7_7_1_3.label: Terrain Aspect, Exposition
LCH-7_7_1_3.tip: Compass direction a slope faces, given in degrees from 0 to 360, where 0 is north, 90 east, 180 south and 270 west.

LCH-8.label: Spatial Characteristics
LCH-8.tip: Groups characteristics describing how things are arranged inside a piece of land, e.g. mixed or uniform patterns, hedgerows or road networks.

LCH-8_1.label: Spatial Distribution Pattern
LCH-8_1.tip: Groups two-dimensional patterns showing how different land cover elements are spread out and relate to each other within an area.

LCH-8_1_1.label: Homogeneous, Evenly Textured
LCH-8_1_1.tip: Area that is uniform throughout, with every spot of the same kind and even texture, e.g. the lawn of a football pitch.

LCH-8_1_2.label: Heterogeneous, Mixed, Unevenly Textured
LCH-8_1_2.tip: Area where several different features are mixed together fairly evenly, giving an uneven, patchy texture, e.g. trees and shrubs intermingled.

LCH-8_1_3.label: Mosaic Pattern
LCH-8_1_3.tip: Area made up of distinct patches, each uniform in itself but clearly different from its neighbours, e.g. a patchwork of small fields.

LCH-8_1_4.label: Scattered Pattern
LCH-8_1_4.tip: A feature that appears only here and there, unevenly spread and not dominant, e.g. scattered trees in a pasture.

LCH-8_1_5.label: Regular Spacing
LCH-8_1_5.tip: Objects arranged at regular, even distances from each other, e.g. houses in a planned housing estate or trees in an orchard.

LCH-8_2.label: Linear Feature Pattern
LCH-8_2.tip: Groups narrow linear landscape features, too small to map one by one, that still shape an area's character, e.g. hedgerows or stone walls.

LCH-8_2_1.label: Hedge Rows
LCH-8_2_1.tip: A plot of land surrounded by or divided by several hedgerows, giving it a sub-divided look; mostly found in farming areas.

LCH-8_2_2.label: Rows of Trees
LCH-8_2_2.tip: A plot of land surrounded by or containing several lines of trees, e.g. windbreaks in the countryside or tree-lined avenues in towns.

LCH-8_2_3.label: Stone Walls
LCH-8_2_3.tip: A plot of land surrounded by or containing several traditional dry stone walls, typical of old farming landscapes.

LCH-8_3.label: Linear Technical Network
LCH-8_3.tip: Groups networks of linear technical structures that run through an area and shape its look, e.g. small roads, ditches, fences or pipelines.

LCH-8_3_1.label: Roads Or Railways
LCH-8_3_1.tip: Shows that an area contains a recognisable network of roads or railways, even if their exact location is not known.

LCH-8_3_2.label: Pipelines
LCH-8_3_2.tip: Shows that an area contains one pipeline or a network of them, even if their exact location is not known.

LCH-8_4.label: Vertical Position
LCH-8_4.tip: Groups the vertical position of an object relative to the ground: on the surface, raised above it, or below it.

LCH-8_4_1.label: On Ground Surface
LCH-8_4_1.tip: An object located directly on the ground surface, e.g. a road at street level.

LCH-8_4_2.label: Suspended, Elevated
LCH-8_4_2.tip: An object raised above the ground or hanging over it, e.g. a bridge, an elevated railway or overhead power lines.

LCH-8_4_3.label: Under Ground
LCH-8_4_3.tip: An object located below the ground surface, e.g. a tunnel, subway line or buried pipe.

LCH-9.label: Object Characteristics
LCH-9.tip: Groups measurements of objects, such as size, how often they occur and when or how long things happen; always used together with another class.

LCH-9_1.label: Geometric Parameters
LCH-9_1.tip: Groups size measurements for objects, such as area, length, width, height and share of an area covered.

LCH-9_1_1.label: Object Area Size
LCH-9_1_1.tip: Size of an object's area in square meters, recorded as a from/to range; for an exact value both ends are the same.

LCH-9_1_1_1.label: Object Area Size Value From
LCH-9_1_1_1.tip: Lower end of the range for an object's area, in square meters.

LCH-9_1_1_2.label: Object Area Size Value To
LCH-9_1_1_2.tip: Upper end of the range for an object's area, in square meters.

LCH-9_1_2.label: Object Length
LCH-9_1_2.tip: Length of an object in meters, recorded as a from/to range; for an exact value both ends are the same.

LCH-9_1_2_1.label: Object Length Value From
LCH-9_1_2_1.tip: Lower end of the range for an object's length, in meters.

LCH-9_1_2_2.label: Object Length Value To
LCH-9_1_2_2.tip: Upper end of the range for an object's length, in meters.

LCH-9_1_3.label: Object Width
LCH-9_1_3.tip: Width of an object in meters, recorded as a from/to range; for an exact value both ends are the same.

LCH-9_1_3_1.label: Object Width Value From
LCH-9_1_3_1.tip: Lower end of the range for an object's width, in meters.

LCH-9_1_3_2.label: Object Width Value To
LCH-9_1_3_2.tip: Upper end of the range for an object's width, in meters.

LCH-9_1_4.label: Object Height
LCH-9_1_4.tip: How tall an object stands above the ground (not height above sea level), in meters, recorded as a from/to range.

LCH-9_1_4_1.label: Object Height Value From
LCH-9_1_4_1.tip: Lower end of the range for an object's height above ground, in meters.

LCH-9_1_4_2.label: Object Height Value To
LCH-9_1_4_2.tip: Upper end of the range for an object's height above ground, in meters.

LCH-9_1_5.label: Area Coverage
LCH-9_1_5.tip: Share of a larger area taken up by a given cover or use, as a percentage range, e.g. trees covering 30 to 40% of a park.

LCH-9_1_5_1.label: Area Coverage Value From
LCH-9_1_5_1.tip: Lower end of the range for the percentage of an area covered by a given cover or use, in %.

LCH-9_1_5_2.label: Area Coverage Value To
LCH-9_1_5_2.tip: Upper end of the range for the percentage of an area covered by a given cover or use, in %.

LCH-9_2.label: Occurrence Type
LCH-9_2.tip: Groups ways of saying how many or how much of something is present in an area, as a percentage, a count or simply as present.

LCH-9_2_1.label: Percentage Occurrence
LCH-9_2_1.tip: Share of certain objects among all distinct objects in an area, given as a percentage range, e.g. the proportion of buildings that are houses.

LCH-9_2_1_1.label: Percentage Occurrence Value From
LCH-9_2_1_1.tip: Lower end of the range for the percentage share of certain objects among all objects in an area, in %.

LCH-9_2_1_2.label: Percentage Occurrence Value To
LCH-9_2_1_2.tip: Upper end of the range for the percentage share of certain objects among all objects in an area, in %.

LCH-9_2_2.label: Countable Occurrence
LCH-9_2_2.tip: Absolute number of certain objects found in an area, recorded as a from/to range, e.g. how many wind turbines stand in a field.

LCH-9_2_2_1.label: Countable Occurrence Value From
LCH-9_2_2_1.tip: Lower end of the range for how many of the objects occur in the area, as a plain count.

LCH-9_2_2_2.label: Countable Occurrence Value To
LCH-9_2_2_2.tip: Upper end of the range for how many of the objects occur in the area, as a plain count.

LCH-9_2_3.label: Present Occurrence
LCH-9_2_3.tip: Simply records that something is present in an area when its exact number or amount cannot be given.

LCH-9_3.label: Temporal Parameters
LCH-9_3.tip: Groups time information about things in an area, such as the date of an event, how long something lasts or how often it recurs.

LCH-9_3_1.label: Instant Event Date
LCH-9_3_1.tip: Date of a sudden, short event that changes the landscape, e.g. a storm, given as the day number counted from 1 January.

LCH-9_3_1_1.label: Instant Event Date Value From
LCH-9_3_1_1.tip: Start of a short time window in which a sudden event happened, given as day of the year.

LCH-9_3_1_2.label: Instant Event Date Value To
LCH-9_3_1_2.tip: End of a short time window in which a sudden event happened, given as day of the year.

LCH-9_3_2.label: Duration
LCH-9_3_2.tip: How long a situation lasts, counted in days, e.g. a crop's growing cycle, a construction site or a flood.

LCH-9_3_2_1.label: Duration Value From
LCH-9_3_2_1.tip: Lower end of the range for how long a situation lasts, in days.

LCH-9_3_2_2.label: Duration Value To
LCH-9_3_2_2.tip: Upper end of the range for how long a situation lasts, in days.

LCH-9_3_3.label: Period
LCH-9_3_3.tip: A span of time bounded by an explicit start date and end date, e.g. the months a field lies fallow.

LCH-9_3_3_1.label: Period Start Date
LCH-9_3_3_1.tip: First day of a period, given as the day number of the year, from 1 for 1 January to 365 for 31 December.

LCH-9_3_3_1_1.label: Period Start Date Value From
LCH-9_3_3_1_1.tip: Earliest possible start of a period, given as day of the year; used when the exact start date is uncertain.

LCH-9_3_3_1_2.label: Period Start Date Value To
LCH-9_3_3_1_2.tip: Latest possible start of a period, given as day of the year; used when the exact start date is uncertain.

LCH-9_3_3_2.label: Period End Date
LCH-9_3_3_2.tip: Last day of a period, given as the day number of the year counted from 1 January.

LCH-9_3_3_2_1.label: Period End Date Value From
LCH-9_3_3_2_1.tip: Earliest possible end of a period, given as day of the year; used when the exact end date is uncertain.

LCH-9_3_3_2_2.label: Period End Date Value To
LCH-9_3_3_2_2.tip: Latest possible end of a period, given as day of the year; used when the exact end date is uncertain.

LCH-9_3_4.label: Recurring Frequency
LCH-9_3_4.tip: How many times per year something changes or repeats, e.g. how often a meadow is mowed.

LCH-9_3_4_1.label: Recurring Frequency Value From
LCH-9_3_4_1.tip: Lower end of the range for how many times per year something recurs, as a plain count.

LCH-9_3_4_2.label: Recurring Frequency Value To
LCH-9_3_4_2.tip: Upper end of the range for how many times per year something recurs, as a plain count.
